commentary.text:
Opening plan: this game is really a race for the four center squares, but a lone piece in the center is fragile — a sandwich only needs two pieces of one color on opposite sides. So I want to occupy the center early with Red and Yellow while keeping the flanking geometry in my favor: because I control two colors, any enemy piece that steps between two of my Red pieces (or two Yellows) can be snapped off immediately.

Red drives straight down the d-file to the top-left center square. This claims a center square on move one, forces Blue or Green to commit a piece toward the middle if they want to contest, and leaves my remaining Red pieces on row 0 free to drop down columns 2 or 5 to form the far end of a sandwich against whatever they put on (3,2) or (3,4). Yellow will mirror from the bottom on my next turn.

Red has jumped straight into the center at (3,3) — the center-occupation win means I can't let Team A quietly assemble all four central squares. My move takes the center square (4,3) with Blue: it plants a permanent blocker on the four-square goal, and it sets up a concrete threat — if the Red piece stays on (3,3), my next Blue move to (2,3) sandwiches it vertically between two Blues. I checked safety: no Red piece can currently reach (5,3) (column 3 is blocked by my own piece and row 5 is empty of Red), so the standard counter-sandwich against my new piece isn't available, and Yellow can never pair with Red to capture.

Blue answered by dropping a piece to (4,3), directly under my Red — that's a bid to sandwich my Red on the d-file by later landing a Blue on (2,3), with (4,3) as the far flank. I note the important rule detail: captures only fire on the moving side's landing, so pre-built flanks don't auto-trigger. That means the way to win material is to keep one flank standing and *walk the second one in*.

Yellow drops to (4,4). Three things at once: it takes a second center square for my team, it puts a Yellow flank on the right of Blue's (4,3), and it sets up a concrete capture — Yellow from (7,2) can run straight up column 2 to (4,2), landing with Yellow already on (4,4), which sandwiches and removes Blue's center piece. Moving into contact here is safe, since a piece is never captured for stepping into a sandwich itself.

Blue's own threat on my Red arrives before that, so on my next Red turn I intend to slide (3,3) sideways to (3,4) — sidestepping the d-file pincer while keeping a center square, and vacating (3,3) so Blue's flank there becomes worthless.

Yellow answered by taking (4,4), and there's a real tactic aimed at me: Yellow (7,2) can run up column 2 to (4,2) and sandwich my Blue piece on (4,3) against the Yellow on (4,4). I also verified that "defending" by putting Green directly on (4,2) loses even more — Yellow lands on (4,1) and captures the whole Green+Blue line against the Yellow flank at (4,4). So instead I block the approach route: Green to (5,2) seals column 2, which is Yellow's only way to reach (4,2) (row 4 from the left is blocked by my own pieces). This keeps my center blocker on (4,3) alive and preserves my main threat — if Red doesn't rescue the piece on (3,3) this turn, Blue plays to (2,3) next and captures it in a vertical sandwich against my Blue on (4,3).

Green's slide to (5,2) cut column 2, killing my planned Yellow run to (4,2). Fine — the more urgent matter is Blue's pincer: with Blue already anchored on (4,3), a Blue landing on (2,3) would sandwich my Red on (3,3) down the d-file, and row 2 is currently a clear highway from (2,7).

So Red drops one square short of the center to (2,4), which is a blocking move disguised as a developing move. It slams the door on row 2 — Blue can no longer slide from (2,7) across to (2,3) — while keeping my Red on (3,3) and Yellow on (4,4) holding two of the four center squares. Blue's flank on (4,3) is now inert.

It also builds my next idea. If Blue tries to plug the last free center square by running (3,7) across to (3,4), that piece walks into a gap between my Red on (3,3) and a Red that can drop down column 5 to (3,5) — landing there snaps the Blue piece off the board. And if Blue leaves (3,4) alone, my Red on (2,4) simply steps down into it, giving my team three center squares with only Blue's (4,3) left to dislodge.

Red's move to (2,4) was a good defensive block — it cuts my row-2 path to (2,3), so the sandwich on the Red center piece is off for now, and landing near it is poisoned (Red at (2,2) or (2,6) would counter-sandwich me). So I switch targets to the Yellow piece on (4,4). Blue to (5,5) does two jobs at once: it threatens Blue (5,5)→(4,5) next turn, which sandwiches Yellow (4,4) against my Blue on (4,3), and it occupies the square Red would want as a staging point (Red (0,5) running down column 5 was the only realistic route to (5,3), from where Red could sandwich my center blocker on (4,3) against Red (3,3)). I checked that (5,5) itself can't be sandwiched in one move by either opponent color. If Yellow retreats the (4,4) piece, Team A's center project collapses; if Red blocks at (4,5) instead, that Red piece and the Yellow together form a line I can later capture wholesale by landing on (4,6) against my (4,3) flank.

Blue's slide to (5,5) is the real threat: with Blue already sitting on (4,3), a Blue step up to (4,5) would sandwich my Yellow on (4,4) between the two Blues and take it off the board. I can't block (4,5) — column 5 is corked by that same Blue piece, and any Red I park there gets sandwiched in turn between (5,5) and a Blue dropping to (3,5).

So Yellow steps up one square to (3,4). This is the square I've been building toward. Look at what flanks it: a sandwich on (3,4) can only come from the pairs (2,4)/(4,4) or (3,3)/(3,5) — and I already own (2,4) and (3,3) with Red. Both pincer pairs are permanently broken as long as those two Reds stay put, so this Yellow is effectively immune to capture where it stands, and it's a center square.

I give up (4,4) for now, but my team still holds two of the four center squares with an uncapturable anchor, and Blue's (4,3) piece has lost the partner it needed. My Reds on (2,4) and (3,3) are now doing double duty: bodyguards for the Yellow and flanks for future captures down column 5 and row 3.

Yellow dodged my sandwich by stepping to (3,4), so Team A now holds two center squares — but the center win still needs (4,3), which my Blue occupies. My job is to make that blocker permanent. The only realistic capture pattern against it is Red landing on (5,3), sandwiching it against Red (3,3). So Green slides from (5,2) to (5,3) and sits on that square for good. This also completely defuses the Yellow pincer that was brewing against my Green on row 5 (Yellow to (5,3) then (5,1)), and vacating column 2 is now harmless because Yellow's old flank on (4,4) is gone — a Yellow piece arriving at (4,2) would have no partner to capture with. One caution I'm logging for future turns: a Red piece landing on (6,3) would sandwich my Green(5,3)+Blue(4,3) pair against Red (3,3), but no Red piece can reach row 6 or column 3 below my wall any time soon, and I'll keep that square guarded.

Green's move to (5,3) looks natural — it shields Blue's (4,3) from below — but it actually stacks two enemy pieces into a single column with my Red already sitting on top at (3,3). That's a capture line waiting to happen: a Red landing on (6,3) would look up column 3 and see Green, then Blue, then my own Red at (3,3) — an unbroken run of non-Red pieces closed off by my own piece. Both of them come off the board in one move.

So Red runs the full length of column 2 down to (6,2), one step away from that square. This is safe where it stands: the vertical pincer on (6,2) is dead because my own Yellow occupies (7,2), and Green has nothing that reaches (6,1) and (6,3) in time.

Now the opponents are on an awkward fork. If Blue slides (4,3) out of the column to save itself, it abandons a center square and my team is one piece from three-quarters of the middle. If Green slides (5,3) away instead, it stops shielding Blue, and the square (5,3) becomes the killing spot for a Red landing there with (3,3) as the far flank. If they do neither, I take two pieces at once — a third of each color's tolerance before elimination.

Meanwhile my row-3 wall of Red(3,3)/Yellow(3,4) with Red(2,4) behind it stays intact, and none of my pieces can be sandwiched in a single move.

Red's slide to (6,2) set up exactly the tactic I was worried about: Red lands on (6,3) next turn and sandwiches my Green (5,3) + Blue (4,3) pair against the Red on (3,3) — a two-piece capture. Rather than defend awkwardly, I sidestep: Blue moves from (4,3) to (4,4). This breaks the sandwich line at its middle (an empty (4,3) kills the capture entirely), keeps my piece on a central square so Team A still cannot complete the four-square center win, and creates a new weapon: my Blue on (4,4) is now the bottom flank of the Red(2,4)+Yellow(3,4) column — if I ever get a Blue piece to (1,4), both of those pieces are captured at once. I know (1,4) is currently poisoned (Red (0,5)→(0,4) would counter-sandwich), so that threat mostly serves to tie Red's (0,5) piece to home. Remaining care points: if Red re-plants a piece on (4,3), the sandwich against my Green (5,3) revives via (6,3) — but that takes two Red moves and Green can block (6,3) or step away in between.

Blue retreated (4,3) to (4,4), dodging my column-3 double capture and planting itself in the last enemy-held center square. That's actually progress for me: (4,3) is now empty, so my team holds two center squares with a third sitting vacant.

Crucially, Blue's new home has a fatal geometry. My Yellow already sits on (3,4), directly above it. A Yellow landing on (5,4) would look up the column and see Blue, then my own Yellow — that's a sandwich, and Blue's center piece dies. I have no Yellow that can reach (5,4) today: column 4 has no Yellow on it, row 5 is corked by Green at (5,3) on one side and Blue at (5,5) on the other.

So Yellow shuffles from (7,5) to (7,4), stepping onto the open column. It's a quiet move but it aims at everything at once. From (7,4) the whole of column 4 is clear: if Blue stays put, my next Yellow turn runs down to (5,4) and takes it; if Blue flees the square to avoid that, the column is open all the way to (4,4) itself and my Yellow simply moves in to claim the center square instead. Either way Blue's piece is being evicted.

The move is also completely safe — (7,4) sits on my home row flanked by my own Yellow on (7,3), so no pincer exists there. Meanwhile my Red wall on (2,4)/(3,3) keeps the Yellow on (3,4) uncapturable, and my Red on (6,2) still watches row 6 and can swing to (5,2) to punish anything that steps onto (4,3) or (5,3).

Yellow's shuffle to (7,4) reveals the plan: run up column 4 and sandwich my Blue (4,4) against the Yellow on (3,4). Column 4 below that Yellow piece is a death lane for me — stacking blockers there only lengthens the line Yellow captures — so the correct block is Blue to (6,4) with a gap at (5,4), which I'll play next Blue turn (the threat only lands after my ply-13 move, so timing works). That frees Green right now for the most valuable square on the board: (4,3). Taking it does three things — it denies Red the natural rebuilding move (3,3)→(4,3), it gives my team two of the four center squares (making Team A's center-occupation win essentially impossible without capturing through me), and it dodges the old (6,3) sandwich geometry entirely since column 3 behind me is now empty. The known cost: Red can aim (6,2)→(5,2)→(5,3) to sandwich my new Green piece against Red (3,3), but that takes two Red moves and Green itself moves in between, so I can always block or step away in time.

Green stepping into (4,3) is a double-purpose move: it grabs the empty center square and, more dangerously, it completes half a pincer on my Red at (3,3). Green only needs to land on (2,3) to snap that Red off the board — and row 2 is a clear highway from Green's piece on (2,0). That capture would also strip a bodyguard from my Yellow on (3,4), so it's the one thing I have to answer.

I can't plug (2,3) with my Red on (2,4), because vacating (2,4) lets Blue run along row 2 into it and sandwich my Yellow against Blue's (4,4). Instead I bring up my last idle back-rank piece: Red from (0,1) drops to (2,1), slamming the door in the middle of Green's approach lane. Green now has no route to (2,3) at all — row 2 is blocked and there's no Green anywhere on column 3 above the middle — so my Red on (3,3) is secure again, and with it the whole row-3 wall.

There's a bonus: Green's piece on (2,0) is now completely frozen, walled in by its own pieces above and below and my Red to its right.

The attacking idea I'm keeping in reserve: my Red on (3,3) is the anchor for a kill on Green's (4,3). Any Red that lands on (5,3) sandwiches it. My Red on (6,2) is two steps from that square via (5,2), so Green's new center piece is living on borrowed time unless it retreats — and if it retreats, the center square opens back up for me.

Now I hold two center squares — Green (4,3) and Blue (4,4) — which locks Team A out of the center win unless they capture through me. The live threat is Yellow (7,4) running to (5,4) and sandwiching my Blue (4,4) against Yellow (3,4). Column 4 under that Yellow piece is a trap lane: any contiguous stack of my pieces there just becomes a longer line for Yellow to capture, so the correct block is Blue to (6,4) leaving (5,4) empty — the gap breaks any sandwich line, and with (6,4) occupied the Yellow piece on (7,4) can no longer enter the column at all (row 5 is unreachable for Yellow). I verified the blocker itself is safe: capturing it would need Yellow on (5,4), which is unreachable, or two Red pieces on row 6 at (6,3) and (6,5), which is several moves away. Red's quiet (0,1)→(2,1) looks like slow maneuvering on the queenside; the concrete Red plan I'm still tracking is (6,2)→(5,2)→(5,3) to sandwich my Green (4,3) against Red (3,3) — Green gets a move before that lands and can block or step aside.

Blue's (6,7)→(6,4) plugged column 4 to stop my Yellow from dropping to (5,4). But look at what that Blue piece has walked into: it now stands between (5,4) and my Yellow on (7,4). Meanwhile Blue's other piece on (4,4) stands between (5,4) and my Yellow on (3,4). The square (5,4) has become a double-kill point — a Yellow landing there looks up and sandwiches Blue(4,4) against my Yellow(3,4), and looks down and sandwiches Blue(6,4) against my Yellow(7,4). Two Blue pieces in a single move, which is two thirds of the way to eliminating the color.

Column 4 is corked, so I approach sideways: Yellow runs up column 3 to (5,3), one step from the killing square. The landing itself is quiet and safe — the pincer pairs on (5,3) are (5,2)/(5,4), which no single color can fill, and (4,3)/(6,3), where Green owns (4,3) but has no way to reach (6,3) with row 6 blocked by my own Red on (6,2).

Blue cannot save both pieces with one turn. Moving (4,4) leaves (6,4) to die; moving (6,4) leaves (4,4) to die; and if Blue plugs (5,4) itself with the piece from (5,5), I bring my last back-rank Yellow up column 6 and take that plug from the other side, since my Yellow on (5,3) becomes the far flank.

There's a quieter dividend too. Green's piece on (4,3) is now squeezed between my Red above and my Yellow below. If it runs, my Yellow on (5,3) simply steps up into (4,3) — giving my team three of the four center squares with only Blue's (4,4) left to evict.

Yellow's move to (5,3) creates serious tactics: it enables Yellow (5,3)→(5,4), which would sandwich-capture BOTH my Blue (4,4) (against Yellow (3,4) above) and my Blue (6,4) (against Yellow (7,4) below), and it also gives Red a brutal option — Red (6,2)→(6,3) would capture my Green (4,3) together with Yellow's own (5,3) against the Red flank on (3,3), a friendly-fire trade Red should happily take. My Green on (4,3) is boxed in (own pieces and enemies on all four lines) except for squares (4,2)/(4,1), so I dodge to (4,2). That single step defuses Red's double capture completely — the sandwich line now has a hole at (4,3), which also kills the "capture both my center pieces" geometry.

The bigger point: I've spotted that Blue (1,7)→(1,4) is an immediate two-piece bomb — the Red (2,4)+Yellow (3,4) column is flanked by my Blue (4,4) below, so landing on (1,4) captures both at once, and the old poison (Red (0,5)→(0,4)) evaporates because the captured pieces vacate the line Red would need. That capture also removes the top flank of Yellow's death-column tactic. If Red doesn't defuse it this turn, Blue fires it next; worst case Yellow still picks off my (6,4) with the (5,4) move, but a two-for-one trade in my favor plus wrecking their center is excellent.

Green abandoned the center, so (4,3) is empty and my double-capture threat on (5,4) is still live: a Yellow landing there takes Blue(4,4) against my Yellow(3,4) and Blue(6,4) against my Yellow(7,4) in one stroke.

Rather than defend, I'm adding a second, independent threat that Blue cannot parry in the same turn. Red runs the full length of column 5 down to (4,5), settling on Blue's other side. Now my Red on (3,3) is one single step from (4,3) — and landing there would look right along row 4 and see Blue(4,4) closed off by my new Red on (4,5). That's a second way to kill the same Blue piece, this time with Reds, and it plants a Red on a center square while doing it.

Blue has one move and three problems. Blocking (5,4) with the piece from (5,5) stops the Yellow fork but leaves (4,4) to be taken by Red stepping into (4,3). Saving (4,4) leaves (6,4) to the Yellow fork. And if Blue instead swings (3,7) across to (3,5) to sandwich my new Red against (5,5), it spends its turn on one piece while my Yellow immediately forks and removes two — a trade of one Red for two Blues that puts Blue one capture away from elimination, since three losses wipes a color out.

The move is safe from Green entirely — every pincer pair around (4,5) is mixed-colour — and my row-3 wall of Red(2,4)/Red(3,3)/Yellow(3,4) stays untouched, so nothing in my center is capturable.

Red ignored my column-4 bomb to plant a piece on (4,5) — creating its own threat (Red (3,3)→(4,3) would sandwich my Blue (4,4) against it). But the bomb fires first, and firing it is clearly best: Blue (1,7)→(1,4) lands and captures BOTH Red (2,4) and Yellow (3,4) immediately — the unbroken enemy line below my landing square runs straight into my own Blue flank on (4,4). That puts Red and Yellow each at 1 loss of 3, and critically it deletes Yellow (3,4), the top flank of the column-4 death lane, so Yellow's follow-up (5,3)→(5,4) now only picks off my (6,4) blocker instead of double-capturing. The old counter-poison (Red 0,5→0,4) is gone twice over — that Red piece moved to (4,5), and the captured pieces vacate the line anyway, so my new piece on (1,4) is safe.

Expected continuation: Yellow probably takes my (6,4) via (5,4); Green will then block (4,3) to protect my center Blue from the Red (4,5) flank, and I'll watch Red's row-6 route to (6,5) against my (5,5). I may bleed a piece or two in the scramble, but I've banked two captures, both enemy colors are one loss from halfway to elimination, and my team still holds the center squares that lock out Team A's instant win.

Blue found a hard shot: dropping (1,7) down to (1,4) turned column 4 into a firing line — my Red on (2,4) and Yellow on (3,4) were an unbroken run of non-Blue pieces closed off by Blue's own piece on (4,4), so both came off at once. That's the friendly-fire clause working against me, and it cost me one piece of each color. I was watching the short pincers and missed the long line. From here I'm checking every rank and file that runs through my pieces for an enemy anchor at the far end before I commit.

The compensation is that Blue's (4,4) anchor is still stuck in place and its piece on (6,4) is now sitting between my Yellow on (5,3)'s destination and my Yellow on (7,4). Yellow steps one square right to (5,4) and looks down the column: Blue on (6,4), then my own Yellow on (7,4) behind it. That Blue piece is captured outright — Blue's first loss.

The landing square is solid. The pincer pairs around (5,4) are (5,3)/(5,5) and (4,4)/(6,4); Blue holds one half of each but has no piece that can reach (5,3), and with (6,4) swept away there's no Blue left on row 6 or able to come down column 4 past its own piece to refill it.

I expect Blue to answer by swinging (3,7) across to (3,5), which sandwiches my Red on (4,5) against Blue's (5,5). That's an even trade of one piece each, and it's not avoidable this turn since no Yellow can reach (3,5) to block. I'll take the free capture now and rebuild the pressure on Blue's center piece afterward.

Yellow took my (6,4) blocker as expected. Now Red has TWO one-move captures queued — (3,3)→(4,3) sandwiching my Blue (4,4), and (6,2)→(6,5) sandwiching my Blue (5,5), both powered by the Red flank on (4,5) — and Green can't parry both. So instead of defending one and losing the other anyway, I counter-punch: Green (4,2)→(2,2) captures the Red piece on (2,1), sandwiched against my Green wall on (2,0). That puts Red at 2 of 3 losses — one more Red capture and Red is eliminated, turning every Red piece into a Void that can never capture again, which would gut Team A's entire offense.

This changes Red's incentives completely. If Red still cashes a Blue capture next turn, it walks the tightrope at 2/3 while I have concrete shots at a third: if my (5,5) survives, Blue (3,7)→(3,5) captures Red (4,5) on the spot (sandwich against (5,5)); my (4,4) is the left flank for a future capture on (4,5) via (4,6); and Green (4,0) can still reach (4,3) to re-block the center. If Red instead turns cautious and pulls (4,5) back to safety, both threats on my Blues evaporate and I've banked a free capture. Either way this beats passive defense, where Red takes a Blue piece for nothing. Score now: Red 2, Blue 1, Yellow 1, Green 0.

Green struck back: (4,2) up to (2,2) sandwiched my Red on (2,1) against Green's own piece on (2,0). Red is now at two losses — one more and the color is eliminated and its survivors turn to Void.

Even so, this is the moment to strike. My Red on (4,5) survived Blue's turn, and that makes (4,3) a killing square: Red steps down from (3,3) into (4,3) and looks right along row 4 — Blue's piece on (4,4), then my own Red on (4,5) behind it. Blue's center piece is captured, taking Blue to two losses, and my Red lands on a center square in the process.

I'm going in with eyes open about the cost. Blue's clearest reply is swinging (3,7) across to (3,5), which sandwiches my Red on (4,5) against Blue's (5,5) and eliminates Red as a color. I accept that, because of what it leaves behind: eliminated Reds become Void pieces that still move and still count toward the four-square center victory, my Yellow is untouched with five pieces, and Blue would be sitting on two losses with its piece on (5,5) already flanked by my Yellow on (5,4). My Yellow on (7,6) has a clear run up column 6 to (5,6), and landing there sandwiches (5,5) against (5,4) — that would be Blue's third loss and wipe the color out.

So the trade I'm inviting is my Red color for Blue's color, and it leaves Green as the only enemy piece on the board still able to capture anything, while my Yellow still can.

The moment has arrived: my Blue on (5,5) is the perfect flank, and Blue (3,7)→(3,5) sandwiches the Red piece on (4,5) against it — Red's third loss, eliminating Red entirely. Every remaining Red piece ((0,6), (4,3), (6,2)) becomes a Void that can never capture again, which destroys Team A's whole attacking engine in one stroke.

I'm clear-eyed about the cost: Yellow can answer with (7,6)→(5,6), capturing my (5,5) against the Yellow on (5,4), which would be Blue's third loss too — my Blues would go Void. I considered retreating (5,5) instead, but then the elimination shot evaporates (it's the flank), and a live Red at two losses with four healthy pieces keeps hunting my two-loss Blue forever. Trading eliminations is clearly favorable: afterwards the capture game is Green (six pieces, zero losses) versus Yellow (five pieces, one loss), and I only need two Yellow captures to win the match outright, while Yellow needs three Greens. My Blue Voids remain valuable as movable blockers — especially for the center, where I must watch Team A's new resource: the Red Void sitting on center square (4,3) still counts for their center-occupation win, so I'll plant a Blue Void on (3,4) or contest (4,4) to keep that locked.

Blue took the bait exactly as expected — (3,7) swung to (3,5) and sandwiched my Red on (4,5) against Blue's (5,5), which pushed Red to three losses and eliminated the color. My three surviving Reds are now Void: they still move and, crucially, they still count as team pieces for the four-square center victory, including the one already parked on the center square (4,3).

Now I collect the other half of that trade. Blue's piece on (5,5) has my Yellow sitting on (5,4) right beside it, and column 6 is completely clear from my back rank. Yellow runs from (7,6) up to (5,6) and looks left: Blue on (5,5), then my own Yellow on (5,4) closing the line. That's a sandwich — Blue's piece is captured, and it is Blue's third loss.

That eliminates Blue as a color. Its three remaining pieces on (1,4), (2,7) and (3,5) turn to Void: they keep moving and keep blocking squares, but they can never capture anything again. From this point Green is the only enemy piece on the board with any teeth, while my Yellow — five pieces, one loss — still has full capturing power.

That's the strategic swing I was playing for. Their offence is halved and mine is intact. My path from here is the center: I already hold (4,3) with a Void Red, my Yellow on (5,4) is one step below (4,4), and (3,3) is reachable by walking my Void Red on (0,6) across the top rank and down the open column 3. I'll need to prise open (3,4), where a Blue Void currently blocks the approaches, but Green alone will find it hard to defend all four squares.

The double elimination resolved as planned: Red and Blue are both out, and the endgame is now Green (six pieces, zero losses) versus Yellow (five pieces, one loss) — I need two Yellow captures to win the match; Yellow needs three Greens. The urgent front is the center-occupation win: the Red Void on (4,3) counts for Team A, Yellow (5,4) can step onto (4,4) any time, and the Red Void on (0,6) can maneuver toward (3,3). I need to claim or block the remaining center squares before they assemble. Green (2,2)→(2,3) starts that: next turn this piece drops into (3,3), arriving strictly before the Red Void can (it needs two moves via row 0 and column 3). My Blue Voids are now blockers — the one on (1,4) already seals column 4 from the north, and depending on how the Red Void routes, I'll either park it on (3,4) or on (1,3) to cut the column-3 approach. Meanwhile Yellow has no capture threats against any Green piece for several moves (its pieces are bottled on rows 5 and 7, and the Void on (6,2) ironically blocks Yellow's column-2 attack lane), so I can afford this positional tempo.

With Blue eliminated, the shape of the game has changed completely. Their three surviving Blue pieces are Void — they still shuffle around and block squares, but they can never capture again. Green is the only enemy piece on the board with teeth, and my Yellow, with five pieces, is the only colour on either side that can still take material.

My winning routes are now both open. The direct one is the centre: I already hold (4,3) with a Void Red, and my Yellow on (5,4) has a clear column above it to both (4,4) and (3,4). The remaining square is (3,3), and that one is awkward — Green sits on (2,3) blocking the approach down column 3, and my own Void Red on (4,3) blocks it from below, so the only way in is sideways along row 3.

So this turn I open that road. The Void Red on (6,2) runs up the clear column 2 to (3,2), placing it a single sideways step from (3,3). Void pieces cannot capture, but they occupy squares and they count as team pieces for the centre victory, which is all this one needs to do.
